paper_title: Video-IFBench: Evaluating Instruction Following of Multimodal LLMs in Video Understanding Scenarios

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown strong performance in video understanding. However, their ability to follow instructions in this domain remains under-explored. Real-world video understanding requires models not only to interpret video content correctly, but also to satisfy diverse user-specified constraints. Existing benchmarks focus primarily on task accuracy rather than instruction adherence, leaving this capability insufficiently evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce Video-IFBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating instruction following in video understanding, where models must satisfy diverse user-specified constraints, including those grounded in visual and audio content. We develop an instruction taxonomy with four templates, including single-task, multi-task, selection, and nested instructions, covering 32 task types and 39 manually designed constraint categories spanning both semantic and format requirements. To reduce annotation cost, we build a semi-automatic data construction pipeline that combines MLLMs, programmatic processing, and human verification, resulting in 1.5K samples. We conduct a large-scale evaluation of more than 20 recent MLLMs and show that video instruction following remains challenging for current models, especially for instructions with many constraints, semantic constraints, or complex conditional structures that require selecting the correct branch or path based on video content. We hope our work will facilitate future research on instruction following in video understanding scenarios.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown strong performance in video understanding. However, their ability to follow instructions in this domain remains under-explored. Real-world video understanding requires models not only to interpret video content correctly, but also to satisfy diverse user-specified constraints. Existing benchmarks focus primarily on task accuracy rather than instruction adherence, leaving this capability insufficiently evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce Video-IFBench, comprehensive benchmark for evaluating instruction following in video understanding, where models must satisfy diverse user-specified constraints, including those grounded in visual and audio content. We develop an instruction taxonomy with four templates, including single-task, multitask, selection, and nested instructions, covering 32 task types and 39 manually designed constraint categories spanning both semantic and format requirements. To reduce annotation cost, we build semi-automatic data construction pipeline that combines MLLMs, programmatic processing, and human verification, resulting in 1.5K samples. We conduct large-scale evaluation of more than 20 recent MLLMs and show that video instruction following remains challenging for current models, especially for instructions with many constraints, semantic constraints, or complex conditional structures that require selecting the correct branch or path based on video content. We hope our work will facilitate future research on instruction following in video understanding scenarios.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Recent Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) [38, 50, 27, 1, 39, 45] have advanced rapidly and achieved strong performance on various video understanding tasks. At the same time, the evaluation of video understanding is rapidly expanding. Existing benchmarks examine diverse capabilities, including temporal understanding [26], spatial intelligence [46], general video analysis [9, 10, 22, 47], long-video comprehension [49, 43], and knowledge-intensive reasoning [17]. However, evaluating video understanding solely through response correctness is increasingly insufficient for real-world applications. An important yet underexplored dimension is instruction following. In practical video understanding scenarios, user requests are often accompanied by explicit requirements related to semantic [23, 40, 36] and format constraints [48, 5, 31] on model responses. They may also vary in structural complexity, from requests that seek single piece of information from the video to multi-aspect requests and conditional instructions: models must identify the correct condition branch or path based on the actual video content, execute the corresponding instructions, and satisfy the associated Preprint. constraints. For example, when analyzing cooking tutorial, user may ask an MLLM to describe only the steps after the ingredients are mixed, and list them in chronological order with timestamps. Therefore, the ability to follow instructions is critical dimension for assessing whether such models can be reliably deployed in real-world scenarios. Despite its practical importance, this capability is not yet adequately evaluated. Existing video benchmarks focus primarily on response correctness [22, 9, 26, 49, 43, 10]. They are not designed to test whether MLLMs faithfully execute complex user instructions. Meanwhile, prior work on instruction-following evaluation focuses mainly on text-only settings [19, 18, 48, 34, 42, 31], or on relatively narrow multimodal settings such as image-based instruction following [5, 33, 14], and controllable video captioning [24]. As result, instruction following in more diverse forms, especially under richer visual/audio-grounded constraints, remains insufficiently explored. To address this gap, we introduce Video-IFBench, comprehensive benchmark for evaluating instruction-following capabilities in video understanding. Video-IFBench contains over 700 videos from public data sources, covering diverse domains with individual durations ranging from 10 seconds to 10 minutes and total duration of approximately 49 hours. We design an instruction taxonomy with four templates, including single-task, multi-task, selection, and nested instructions, covering 32 manually curated video understanding task types and 39 semantic or format response constraints. To reduce annotation cost, we develop semi-automatic data construction pipeline that combines MLLM-powered extraction of global and fine-grained local video information, multi-stage complex instruction and checklist generation driven by both MLLMs and programmatic rules, and rigorous human verification, resulting in 1.5K high-quality samples. Beyond data construction, we design an evaluation protocol that combines LLM-as-Judge with programmatic verification, and conduct large-scale empirical study on more than 20 recent MLLMs. Our results show that even the strongest video MLLMs in our evaluation still leave substantial room for improvement in instruction following, with the best model achieving only 54.5% overall score. We further find that models struggle particularly with instructions that involve many constraints, semantic constraints, and complex conditional structures that require matching the correct branch or path based on video content. These findings suggest that strong video understanding accuracy does not automatically translate into faithful adherence to user intent. We therefore argue that instruction following should be treated as first-class evaluation dimension for video MLLMs. In summary, this work makes the following contributions: We introduce Video-IFBench, new benchmark for video instruction following, containing 1.5K high-quality samples over more than 700 videos with diverse instruction structures, tasks, and constraints. We design hybrid evaluation protocol that combines LLM-as-Judge with programmatic verification to assess models performance on video instruction following. We evaluate more than 20 recent MLLMs and show that current models still struggle with strict video instruction following, especially under many constraints, semantic constraints, and conditional instructions.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: 2.1 Instruction-Following Evaluation on LLMs. Instruction-following evaluation has been widely studied in text-only settings. Benchmarks such as FollowEval [19], FollowBench [18], IFEval [48], and InFoBench [34] evaluate whether models satisfy explicit and structured instruction requirements. Later work further studies more complex and realistic settings, including compositional constraints [42], real-user multi-constraint instructions [25], unseen constraints [31], sequential or multi-turn instructions [4, 15, 21], and agentic tasks [32, 3].

sections.title: 2.2 Multimodal Instruction Following.
sections.content: Recent benchmarks extend instruction-following evaluation to multimodal inputs. MIA-Bench [33], MM-IFEngine [5], VC-IFEval [14], MMMT-IF [6], and MCIF [30] evaluate instruction following across image, speech, dialogue, and crosslingual settings. In the video domain, IF-VidCap [24] 2 Figure 1: The data construction pipeline of Video-IFBench. Each curated video is annotated with global description and fine-grained timestamped facts, which are used to generate Single/Multi instructions and condition-based Selection/Nested instructions. Each instruction is paired with checklist for LLM-based or programmatic verification. More examples are provided in Appendix D. studies constrained video captioning. In contrast, our work evaluates instruction following across broader video understanding tasks and more complex instruction structures.

sections.title: 2.3 Video Understanding Benchmarks.
sections.content: Existing video understanding benchmarks evaluate temporal understanding, long-video comprehension, knowledge-intensive reasoning, robustness, and streaming interaction, including MVBench [22], Video-MME [9], TempCompass [26], Video-MMMU [17], MLVU [49], MMVU [47], LongVideoBench [43], PerceptionComp [23], Video-MME-v2 [10], PhoStream [28], and OVOBench [29]. These benchmarks primarily measure response correctness, but provide limited evaluation of whether models can faithfully follow complex user instructions with multiple constraints and conditional structures.

sections.title: 3.1 Benchmark Design
sections.content: To comprehensively evaluate the video instruction-following ability of MLLMs, we design an instruction taxonomy with four instruction templates: Single, Multi, Selection, and Nested. These target two key dimensions of instruction complexity: task composition and conditional structure. Single and Multi. Single and Multi instructions vary task-level composition. Single instruction contains one task that asks for specific piece of information from the video, together with set of response constraints. We use this template to study how performance changes as the number of 3 (a) Instruction types. (b) Video domains and durations. Figure 2: Dataset-level statistics of Video-IFBench. constraints increases, with constraint counts ranging from 1 to 15. In contrast, Multi instruction contains two or more tasks and requires the model to retrieve or reason over multiple pieces of video information in single request. Its constraints may apply either globally to the entire response or locally to specific tasks. To focus on the effect of task count, we keep the number of global and task-specific constraints relatively small, mostly no more than three. Selection and Nested. Selection and Nested instructions evaluate whether models can follow video-grounded conditions. In Selection, the model chooses the correct conditional branch from several candidate branches and executes the corresponding instruction. Nested further organizes such conditions into tree structure, requiring the model to follow the correct path before answering.

sections.title: 3.2 Dataset Construction
sections.content: As shown in Fig. 1, our pipeline includes video curation, task and constraint pool construction, information extraction, instruction generation, checklist generation, and human verification. We collect and filter public videos, build task and constraint pools, and extract global description and fine-grained timestamped facts for each video. These annotations are then used to generate Single/Multi instructions and condition-based Selection/Nested instructions. We further generate checklists for automatic evaluation and manually verify the constructed samples. Video Curation. We collect videos from diverse public sources, including existing video understanding benchmarks (WorldSense [16], Video-MME [9], MMBench-Video [7], FineVideo [8], and LongVALE [11]). We also use set of manually designed keywords to retrieve additional videos from public platforms, covering ten domains. To ensure visual quality, we use MUSIQ [20] to filter out blurred videos. The domain and duration distributions are shown in Fig. 2b. Task and Constraint Pool Construction. We analyze samples from existing video understanding benchmarks [9, 16, 11, 7, 17] and group representative tasks into six high-level categories (Perception & Recognition, Temporal Understanding, Spatial Understanding, Relationship & Interaction, Logical Reasoning, Captioning). For each category, we manually define multiple concrete task types, each with task name, brief description, and example questions. This design improves task diversity over directly prompting MLLMs to generate questions. The full task taxonomy is reported in Appendix B. We construct the constraint pool by reusing and extending format constraints from prior instructionfollowing benchmarks [48, 5, 31], and designing semantic constraints that capture video-specific requirements (e.g., temporal scope, relations). After multiple rounds of manual cleaning to remove ambiguous, redundant, or hard-to-verify constraints, we obtain 39 constraint types, including 22 semantic and 17 format constraints. The full constraint taxonomy is provided in Appendix C. Information Extraction. For each video, we use an MLLM to extract information at two granularities: global description of the overall content and fine-grained facts list. Each fact is defined as an atomic, timestamped visual or audio statement grounded in video content. For longer videos, extracting the full facts list at once often produces coarse and incomplete annotations. We therefore split each long video into one-minute segments and process them sequentially. At each step, we prompt the MLLM to extract local facts and update shared entity memory. This helps keep references to people and objects consistent across segments. 4 (a) Constraint distribution. (b) Instruction structure statistics. Figure 3: Instruction and constraint statistics of Video-IFBench. Single and Multi Instruction Generation. We sample one or more tasks according to the target instruction type and prompt the MLLM to generate instructions from the video description, facts list, and sampled constraints. To avoid repetitive constraint patterns, we sample constraints from predefined count ranges and limit how often each constraint type can appear, which helps balance both constraint types and counts in the generated data. Examples of Single and Multi instructions are shown in Figs. 811 in Appendix D. Selection and Nested Instruction Generation. Directly prompting an MLLM to generate Selection and Nested instructions often fails to produce sufficiently complex branching or nested structures. We therefore use multi-stage pipeline that constructs the conditional structure before generating branch or leaf instructions. As shown in the top-left of Fig. 1, we first transform facts into true and false variants to construct conditions. Then, the MLLM generates three transformations: an edit transformation that minimally changes the fact into false variant (e.g., keyboard screen), negation transformation that negates the original fact (e.g., pours water does not pour water), and combined transformation that edits and negates the fact simultaneously to produce another true variant. We then generate the instruction structure and sample one leaf as the unique true target. For each non-target leaf path, we randomly mark one intermediate node as false if the path does not already contain false node. This ensures that each Selection or Nested instruction has exactly one valid branch or root-to-leaf path. The MLLM then writes the condition text for each intermediate node and generates constrained instruction for each leaf node. Examples of Selection and Nested instructions are shown in Figs. 12 and 13, respectively. Checklist Generation. During instruction generation, we record all constraints sampled for each instruction and pair each constraint with checklist item. Given the instruction and the constraint definition, we prompt the MLLM to generate binary checklist query, where yes indicates that the constraint is satisfied. For semantic constraints, we also generate video-grounded judge context as evidence for evaluation. Human Verification. We manually verify and clean all generated samples. Annotators check video descriptions and facts, instruction constraints, conditional branches or paths, and checklist queries and judge contexts. Problematic samples are corrected or discarded. The final distributions of instruction types, constraints, and instruction structures are shown in Fig. 2a, Fig. 3a, and Fig. 3b.

sections.title: 3.3 Evaluation Paradigm
sections.content: We evaluate model responses with hybrid checklist-based protocol that combines LLM-as-Judge and programmatic verification. Since sample may contain multiple candidate instructions under conditional structures, we define the active instruction as the instruction that should be executed. For 5 Single and Multi samples, the given instruction is directly active. For Selection and Nested samples, only the instruction under the correct branch or path is active. We then evaluate the responses at two levels. Task-level coverage checks whether the response addresses all required tasks in the active instruction; for conditional instructions, this stage is especially useful because it measures whether the model follows the correct branch or path. Constraint-level adherence is evaluated using the checklist items associated with the active instruction. Each checklist item is judged either by an LLM, using the checklist query and judge context, or by deterministic verifier for constraints that can be verified programmatically, e.g., length, format, and keywords. For each sample i, let ti {0, 1} denote task-level coverage, ni denote the number of checklist items, and cij {0, 1} denote whether the j-th item is satisfied. sections.title: 4.1 Settings
sections.content: We conduct an evaluation on frontier proprietary and open-source models, including Gemini-3Pro&Flash [13], GPT-5.4 [37], Doubao [2], the Gemma 4 series [12], the InternVL 3.5 series [41], the Qwen-Omni series [44, 45], the Qwen3-VL series [1], and the Qwen3.5 series [35]. For Gemini and Doubao, we provide videos at 1 FPS; for GPT-5.4, we sample 50 frames due to API constraints. For each open-source model, we follow the recommended inference setup to ensure representative evaluation. We feed the original video with audio to omni-modal models, and provide visiononly models with video frames and timestamped subtitles transcribed by Gemini-3-Pro. In the main experiments, we use Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-Instruct [35] as the judge model. To examine the effect of judge model choice, we also report results with smaller Qwen3.5-35B-A3B judge in the Appendix A.1. The results show that both settings lead to consistent trends. Subsequent analyses are based on the Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-Instruct judge.

sections.title: 4.2 Main Results
sections.content: Overall results. Table 1 reports the main results on Video-IFBench. Gemini-3-Pro achieves the strongest overall performance, with 76.5 TCSR and 54.5 TISR. Among open-source models, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-Think performs best, reaching 69.6 TCSR and 46.1 TISR and leaving gap of 6.9 TCSR points and 8.4 TISR points to Gemini-3-Pro, respectively. Across all models, TISR is consistently lower than TCSR, indicating that models often satisfy some constraints but fail to meet all requirements in an instruction. The results also reveal clear differences across instruction types. Many models achieve higher scores on Multi instructions than on Single instructions, indicating that the main bottleneck is not necessarily handling multiple tasks in one request, but rather following numerous and complex constraints. The challenge becomes more pronounced for Selection and Nested instructions, where models must first select the correct branch or path based on video content before executing the corresponding instruction. Nested instructions are particularly difficult: even Gemini-3-Pro obtains only 53.7 TCSR and 46.0 TISR, while the best open-source model reaches 33.0 TCSR and 28.2 TISR. And within the same model family, larger models generally exhibit better performance, as shown in Fig. 5a.

sections.title: 4.3.3 Depth Sensitivity in Nested Instructions
sections.content: We analyze depth sensitivity on Nested instructions using the same representative models. As shown in Fig. 6, task pass rate generally decreases as the maximum tree depth increases. The drop is clear for strong models: Gemini-3-Pro decreases from 64.6% at depth 2 4 to 55.6% at depth 814, while Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-Think drops from 40.5% to 22.2%. Weaker opensource models remain low across all depth ranges, suggesting that they already struggle with shallow nested structures. These results show that deeper instruction trees make it harder for models to recognize the correct conditional path. Figure 6: Depth sensitivity on Nested instructions.

sections.title: 4.3.4 Branch Number and Position in Selection Instructions
sections.content: We conduct controlled ablation studies on the 3-condition-plus-else subset to study how branch count and correct-branch position affect performance on Selection instructions. For branch count analysis, we keep the correct branch unchanged and progressively add one or two false branches together with the else branch, resulting in 2, 3, and 4-branch variants. For position analysis, we keep the same set of condition branches but move the correct branch to different positions. As shown in Table 3, increasing the number of candidate branches generally lowers task pass rate. For example, Gemini-3-Flash drops from 66.7% with two branches to 56.5% with four branches, and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-Instruct drops from 58.0% to 39.1%. This suggests that models become less reliable as they must compare more video-grounded conditions. We find that the correct-branch position has clear impact. Most models show preference for the first branch, with performance decreasing when the correct branch appears later. For example, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-Think drops from 76.5% at position 1 to 52.9% at position 3, while its Instruct counterpart drops from 70.6% to 29.4%. These results indicate that current models do not evaluate conditional branches equally and may rely on positional biases.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduce Video-IFBench, benchmark for evaluating instruction following in video understanding, with hybrid protocol combining LLM-as-Judge and programmatic verification. Experiments show that current MLLMs struggle with constraint-rich and conditional video instructions. We hope 9 Video-IFBench will facilitate future research on video MLLMs that can faithfully follow complex, constraint-rich instructions in practical applications.

sections.title: A Additional Experimental Results
sections.content: A.1 Main results using Qwen3.5-35B-A3B as Judge Model. To examine the effect of judge model choice, we re-evaluate all model responses using Qwen3.535B-A3B as the judge. Table 4 reports the resulting scores. The values in parentheses in the Overall columns denote the difference from the main results in Table 1. Using smaller judge generally increases the absolute scores, but the relative trends remain largely consistent with the main results, supporting the robustness of our evaluation protocol. A.2 Effect of Thinking Mode on Video-IFBench. As shown in Fig. 7, thinking mode brings clear gains for Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 models, but yields little improvement or even performance drops for InternVL3.5. We hypothesize that the model-dependent effect may be related to how instruction-following rewards are designed during reinforcement learning. Moreover, the gains are generally larger on semantic constraints than on format constraints, suggesting that thinking-style inference is more helpful when constraint following requires visual or audio semantic understanding. 14 Figure 7: Effect of thinking mode on semantic and format constraints.

sections.title: B Task Taxonomy
sections.content: Table 5: Video understanding task taxonomy in Video-IFBench. Category Perception & Recognition Perception & Recognition Perception & Recognition Perception & Recognition Perception & Recognition Perception & Recognition Perception & Recognition Perception & Recognition Perception & Recognition Temporal Understanding

sections.title:
Temporal
Understanding
sections.content: Task Type Entity Recognition Action Recognition Description To describe specific objects, individuals, animals, or elements present within the video frames. To classify the specific movements, gestures, or activities being performed by entities in the video. Attribute Recognition Scene Description To describe specific properties or characteristics of an entity, such as its color, size, shape, or material. To recognize and describe the global environment, setting, or background where the video takes place. Text Recognition (OCR) To detect, extract, and read visible text within the video, Dialogue Recognition Counting Emotion Recognition such as street signs, subtitles, documents, or labels. To recognize and describe spoken content, speaker turns, or dialogue exchanged in the video. To determine how many times target speech pattern occurs or how many target objects appear throughout the video. To infer the emotional state, mood, or facial expressions of the people or characters in the video. Event Recognition To categorize the overarching macroscopic event or social activity happening in the video clip. Event Grounding To pinpoint the exact start and end timestamps of specific event or action, including all instances of its occurrence. Occurrence Localization To locate the precise time interval when an entity, action, or state appears for the first, last, or N-th time.

sections.title: Temporal Ordering
sections.content: To determine the chronological sequence of two or more distinct actions or events.

sections.title:
Temporal Adjacent
Retrieval
sections.content: To retrieve the event or action that occurs immediately preceding or following specified anchor event.

sections.title:
Local Temporal
Understanding
sections.content: To sequentially narrate the list of actions or events that take place within strictly defined time window.

sections.title: Temporal Sorting
sections.content: To logically reorder randomized or shuffled list of video events into their correct chronological sequence.

sections.title: Duration Estimation
sections.content: To calculate or estimate the length of time specific action, event, or state persists. Example Question What type of vehicle is parked in front of the house at 0:15? What is the man in the blue shirt doing when the black car stops? What color is the backpack the child is carrying? Count the number of scenes appeared in the video and describe each of them in detail. What does the neon sign above the shop door say? What are the exact words the news anchor says right after the loud crash is heard? How many times does the host say thank you in the video? Does the woman look happy or frustrated when she opens the cardboard box? Describe, in chronological order, the events experienced by the man wearing red in the video. At what exact timestamps does the dog bark during the video? When does the blue car appear for the third time in the footage? Did the character put on his hat before or after he picked up the umbrella? What happens immediately after the glass shatters on the floor? List all the actions performed by the chef between 1:00 and 1:30 in chronological order. Given the events eating dinner, cooking food, and washing dishes, order them as they actually occurred in the video. How many seconds does the traffic light remain red? 15 Category Temporal Understanding Task Type Audio Change Temporal Understanding Audio-Visual Temporal Alignment Spatial Understanding Relative Direction Judgment Description To identify and describe how spoken audio evolves over time, such as changes in active speaker, speaking state, turn-taking, or stretches of silence. To determine and describe the temporal correspondence between spoken audio cues and visual events, identifying which utterances or speaker turns align with which visible actions, moments, or scene transitions. To determine the directional position of an entity relative to the cameras viewpoint or another reference entity. Spatial Understanding Relative Distance Comparison To compare and determine which entity is closer to or further from given reference point. Spatial Understanding Spatial Relationship Judgment To classify the spatial relations between entities, such as inside, on, under, beside, or attached to. Spatial Understanding Perspective-based Spatial Judgment To reinterpret spatial relationships from hypothetical or shifted orientation (e.g., standing at facing Y). Relationship & Interaction Entity Interaction Recognition Relationship & Interaction Action-Entity Binding To describe dynamic interactions between multiple entities, such as holding, passing, attacking, talking, or hugging. To accurately associate actions with their specific agents and targets to determine who did what to whom. Relationship & Interaction Speech Source Recognition To visually localize the source of spoken audio, such as identifying which person in crowd is speaking. Logical Reasoning Causal Reasoning To deduce the cause-and-effect relationship between different events, actions, or states in the video. Logical Reasoning Counterfactual Reasoning To imagine and reason about alternative outcomes if Logical Reasoning Multi-hop Reasoning specific past event had not occurred or happened differently. To answer complex queries by synthesizing evidence across multiple timestamps, events, or logical steps. Logical Reasoning Knowledge Transfer To extract rule, concept, or physical principle shown in the video and apply it to new, unseen hypothetical scenario. Captioning Segmented Captioning Captioning Dense Captioning

sections.title: Video Summarization
sections.content: To generate individual, coherent textual descriptions for pre-defined or uniformly segmented time intervals of the video. To generate highly detailed, fine-grained descriptions covering all visible actions, entities, and micro-events throughout the video. To generate concise, high-level overview that captures the core theme, main plot, or key highlights of the entire video. Example Question Describe how the active speaker changes from the beginning of the video to the end. Describe which visible actions coincide with the moments when the host starts speaking. Describe the clothing of all people to the left of the entrance. Order the oak tree, park bench, motorcycle, and statue from farthest to nearest relative to the black trash can. Describe the cats spatial relationship to the table, chair, rug, and fireplace while it is sleeping in the video. If you are standing at the doorway facing the window, describe all the objects on your left-hand side and their relative positions. How do the two players interact immediately after the goal is scored? Describe the attributes of the player who passes the basketball to the player wearing yellow jersey. Which person on screen is speaking when the announcement is heard? Why did the fire alarm go off in the hallway? If the man hadnt dropped his keys on the sidewalk, would he have missed the bus? Based on the ingredients the chef gathered at the start and the cooking method used in the middle, what specific dish will be plated at the end? Based on the physics principle demonstrated with the pendulum in the video, what would happen if the string were twice as long? Provide descriptive caption for the events occurring between 0:00-0:30, 0:30-1:00, and 1:00-1:30. Provide dense, second-by-second narrative of every action happening in this street view camera footage. Write two-sentence summary of the main story and outcome shown in this short film.

sections.title: C Constraint Taxonomy
sections.content: Table 6: Constraint taxonomy in Video-IFBench.

sections.title: Temporal Anchor
sections.content: Description Restrict the task to evidence, entities, events, or judgments within specified absolute or segment-defined time window of the video, such as timestamp range, beginning/middle/end portion, or last seconds. Constrain target relative to one explicit reference event, action, state, or timestamp, such as before, after, during, or at the moment of that anchor. Example Use only the visual events that occur in the last 10 seconds of the video in your answer. Mention only the video content before the door opens. 16 Group Semantic Constraint Type Temporal Order Relation Semantic Event Stage Semantic Duration Constraint Semantic Temporal Granularity Description Require the response to determine or preserve temporal ordering relation among two or more already-specified events or targets, such as whether one happens before, after, between, or immediately adjacent to another. Restrict the target to an intrinsic phase of single continuous event or process, such as onset, peak, hold, completion, or recovery, rather than an arbitrary external time window. Require the target event, state, relation, or occurrence to satisfy duration condition such as minimum length, maximum length, longest, shortest, brief, or sustained. Constrain the temporal unit used in the answer to specified granularity, such as seconds only, minutes only, or shot indices only. Semantic Semantic Spatial Region Restriction Relative Spatial Relation Restrict valid candidates to designated region. Select or interpret the target based on its spatial relation to another object, person, landmark, or scene element. Semantic Viewpoint Condition Require the judgment to be made only under specified camera view, shot type, or visual perspective when interpretation depends on viewpoint. Semantic Category Filter Restrict valid targets to specified semantic category or predefined set of categories. Semantic Entity Filter Semantic Attribute Avoidance Semantic Attribute Mention Requirement Semantic Semantic Action-Relative Selection Action Mention Requirement Semantic Action Avoidance Semantic Counting Scope Require the valid entity or speaker targets mentioned in the answer to satisfy specified attribute, appearance property, acoustic trait, or state qualifier. Restrict the output from mentioning specific attributes, physical traits, acoustic traits, or sensitive characteristics of the entities. Require the answer to explicitly mention one or more specified attributes, appearance properties, acoustic traits, or state descriptors for each relevant entity or speaker mentioned in the response, rather than only selecting targets by those attributes. Restrict valid targets to those participating in specified action, interaction, role, or event involvement condition. Require the answer to explicitly mention one or more specified actions, interactions, or motion types performed by designated entity, entity group, body part, or target set, optionally covering all valid instances rather than merely identifying participants. Restrict the answer from mentioning specified actions, interactions, or motion types associated with designated entity, entity group, body part, instrument, or target set, even if those actions are visible in the video. Constrain how many valid items, entities, events, or occurrences should be returned or counted, such as exactly k, at most k, all, or one.

sections.title: Output Ordering
sections.content: Focus on the boundary where presence, state, relation, or scene status changes, such as appears, disappears, turns on, becomes inside, or shifts environment. Require outputs to follow specified ordering rule such as chronological order, reading order, numeric order, order of appearance, or speaker-turn order.

sections.title:
Normalized Value
Format
sections.content: Constrain scalar, label, date, string, or top-k outputs to specified normalized representation without imposing full table, list, or JSON structure.

sections.title: Format
sections.content: Structured JSON Output Require the answer to be valid JSON object or JSON array,

sections.title: Format
sections.content: Closed-Set Option Output optionally with required top-level keys or fixed schema skeleton. Require the answer to be presented as table with an explicit row-column structure, such as Markdown table or CSV-style table. Require the answer to be organized as an ordered list or bullet list rather than free-form paragraph. Require the answer to be exactly one option from provided closed set, optionally with no extra explanation. Example Indicate the temporal order of all mentioned visual events in your answer. Do not mention any video content after the man leaves the room in your answer. Mention only actions lasting more than 2 seconds. Use shot numbers for every mentioned visual segment in your answer; do not use other timestamps. Do not mention any outdoor content in your answer. For all stationary objects mentioned in your answer, describe their spatial relationships relative to the leftmost streetlight at the 3-second mark of the video. From birds-eye view, describe the positions of all objects mentioned in the answer. In the answer, only food-related entities may be mentioned; all other entities must be replaced with uppercase English letters starting from C. Mention only people wearing red jackets in the answer. Do not mention any persons gender or age in the answer. For every person mentioned in the answer, include the color of their pants. Only mention players who were involved in passing in the answer. The answer must include all actions performed by the woman in the video. Do not mention any actions performed by the womans hands in the answer. Only two people may be explicitly mentioned in the answer; all others must be referred to using uppercase English letters. The answer must include every moment when the man in blue enters or exits the frame. All objects mentioned in the answer must be ordered from farthest to nearest relative to the man. Return dates in [YYYY-MM-DD] format. Return the answer as JSON object with keys reason and evidence_segments. Summarize each stage in two-column table. List the key events as an ordered list. Answer with exactly one of: yes, no, unknown. Group Format Format Format Format Format Format Format Format Constraint Type Response Language Response Length Constraint Paragraph Count Constraint List Item Count Constraint Title Requirement Required Keyword Inclusion Description Require the entire answer to be produced in specified language or bilingual pair. Constrain the overall answer length by an exact value, lower bound, an upper bound, or closed range, typically measured in words, or in project-defined Chinese length units for Chinese responses. Require the answer to contain specified number of paragraphs or paragraph-like blocks. Require list-style answer to contain exactly or at most specified number of bullet items or numbered items.
